items.title: ‘Chilling’: As Nepal Grapples With Flooding Chaos, Christians Face Another Potential Horror
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Pray.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

As Nepal deals with the horrific toll of tragic flooding that killed more than 1,000 people, at least 20 churches have reportedly been destroyed by the damaging waters.

Joel Veldkamp, head of international communications at Christian Solidarity International (CSI), told CBN News that one congregation has 80 individuals and families who lost their homes — and that’s just one example.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

CSI has been working to get food, mattresses, mosquito nets, cleaning supplies, and other items to people in Nepal to help meet basic needs.

Veldkamp said there’s another dynamic unfolding inside the South Asian nation: persecution, an issue gaining steam and attention before the deadly flooding began.

“We’ve seen in the last 10 years … persecution of Christians has spiked in Nepal,” he said. “It wasn’t really a big problem before, and today it’s still not on the scale like we’ll see in India, or Pakistan, or other nearby countries. But there is now a law against conversion, so it’s illegal to try to get someone else to change their religion.”

Veldkamp said this is a violation of human rights standards, but that this law is used to prosecute pastors and missionaries — even Christians who might happen to visit and speak with Hindu friends.

“We have seen an uptick in these cases of Christians being jailed on accusations,” he said, noting that sharing the Gospel can be enough to spark legal chaos.

Veldkamp said there’s a new government in Nepal after the previous regime was overthrown in a revolution. An election unfolded in March, which has only added to the uncertainty.

“We still don’t know really what that means, but the country is in flux [and] is headed in a new political direction,” he said. “There are some good signs and some bad signs from the new government, so Christians in Nepal are very concerned about which way the country is going to go now.”

Nepal is one of two Hindu-majority nations in the world, with India joining it in that distinction. Until 2008, Nepal was a Hindu nation before becoming a federal republic. Today, there are new calls to return to that previous designation — something that should be of concern to Christians and other religious minorities.

India has been reportedly putting pressure on Nepal to embrace Hindu nationalism, funding groups that seek to push Christians to reconvert, among other issues.

“There are serious efforts to change Nepal’s constitution to make it officially a Hindu country again,” Veldkamp said. “And in the current environment, that would mean probably the harassment of Christians. Attacks on churches would only increase because then it would be official that this country does not belong to Christians.”

With pastors, missionaries, and Christians already under fire, he said there’s a “real threat that is having a chilling effect” on believers in Nepal.

“Right now, when these things happen to Christians, Christians can say, ‘Hey, we’re a secular country. Nepal is a country for everyone. It says so in our Constitution,'” Veldkamp said. “And that’s … a good argument. That’s a good lever that they can use to appeal to their fellow Nepali citizens for justice.”

But if Nepal becomes a Hindu nation, these arguments dissipate both legally and in the public sphere. Veldkamp encouraged believers worldwide to pray for the church.

items.title: Pro-Life Group Reportedly Kicked Out of Coffee Shop, Compared to KKK
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an Idaho coffee shop after the owner learned she was holding a meeting there.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Kristan Hawkins, president of Students for Life of America, shared a video of what purportedly took place at Wydaho Roasters last month — and that video went viral.

Hawkins told CBN News that coffee shop owner Jim Sheehan made his displeasure known after she, her son, and others met to discuss pro-life issues inside Wydaho Roasters. Her son’s goal has been to rally people against Proposition 1, an abortion measure that will be on the ballot in November.

“We’re recruiting door knockers, and we’ve had students going door to door, educating people in Idaho about this extreme abortion ballot referendum, which sadly many people don’t know about,” Hawkins said, noting her son rallied people online to come meet to form a pro-life group to address the issue.

The coffee shop was the intended gathering place for the group’s first meeting, but that didn’t go very well.

“We had purchased our drinks and our food,” she said. “Some other leaders, community members, came to kind of join the group that I knew from church.”

According to Hawkins, Sheehan came out of his office and told the group they couldn’t meet at the shop and needed to leave. Hawkins took out her camera and started filming the interaction, hoping she could simply convince the owner to let them stay for the first meeting and then pledge not to return.

“I was trying to negotiate with him, just like, let us finish this meeting; we won’t come back,” she said. “And then he just kept going and then compared us to the KKK and said, we were like the KKK, that pro-lifers were like the KKK, which was just beyond the pale. And that’s actually why I decided to release the video.”

Hawkins made it clear that she believes, as an owner, Sheehan has the right to refuse service and was within his rights to ask the group to leave. That said, she also believes in her right to expose his purported comparison between the pro-life activists and the KKK.

The result of the entire escapade was intense media coverage and viral video discussion. Ultimately, both Hawkins and Sheehan reportedly started getting death threats.

“He was well within his rights to kick us out,” Hawkins said. “I was within my rights to expose his insanity, believing that community members were like the KKK, but neither of us deserves to die or receive death threats.”

Sheehan told Fox News that he pushes back on claims the group was kicked out. He said he had asked via Facebook the day before that the group not meet in his coffee shop.

“Sunday she announced on a local community page they were holding this meeting at our business, naming it — I responded to the post politely asking them not to use our business as the agenda of the organization does not align with us,” he told the outlet. “They showed up anyway.”

items.title: SEU Worship Has a Question About Worship Music: Where Did the Joy Go?
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: Chelsea Plank didn’t want “The Cost Is a Joy” on this album. The song came out of a writing session with Cam Giddens and Austin Shuffit, who produces for the group, and when the session ended, what Plank had was an acoustic demo. For her, that’s close to useless. “I nee
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Chelsea Plank didn’t want “The Cost Is a Joy” on this album.

The song came out of a writing session with Cam Giddens and Austin Shuffit, who produces for the group, and when the session ended, what Plank had was an acoustic demo. For her, that’s close to useless.

“I need a fully produced-out track at the end of a writing session,” she said. “I don’t have much vision up here when it comes to, like, man, this acoustic track — I’m just not sure how it lands.”

So when the group sat down early in the year to sort through what might make the record, Plank didn’t put it forward. Other people did.

“They were like, let’s just try this out,” she said. “And it has actually been the anthem of my heart now.”

It’s also the song with her name on it. “The Cost Is a Joy” is credited to SEU Worship and Chelsea Plank, and it hands Found in the Field — the group’s new live album, out now — both its argument and its title.

The argument started with something Shuffit had been noticing in Southeastern University’s students. He came up through the school himself before joining staff, and he prefaced the thought carefully.

“This is no shade towards anyone,” he said, at which point Plank cut in: “Gosh, I don’t know what he’s about to say.”

“There is a lot of language around the cost of following Jesus,” he continued. “The suffering of it, the hardship of it. And we just thought it was a fresh and important perspective for our students to have — that yes, there is suffering, but there is joy in this.”

Plank grew up on that language too, and she doesn’t think it’s wrong.

“It is such a powerful message,” she said. “Even when you hear David talking about, I’m not going to give the Lord an offering that costs me nothing. There is a price to following Jesus. It’s your whole life.”

The problem is what happens when the price is all anyone sings about.

“It can turn really legalistic really quick,” she said.

Her alternative puts the events in a different order. The surrender doesn’t come first and the joy doesn’t arrive later as a reward for it — the seeing comes first, and the giving-up follows from it almost as a reflex. “Out of the abundance of our heart of seeing him, of needing to know him — that’s easy. I will give up everything, and the cost is a joy.”

She has a line for this: “The kingdom of heaven is made up of righteousness, peace and joy. Joy is a third of the kingdom. Joy is the serious business of heaven, we like to say.”

The album title comes from the same place — the parable in Matthew where the kingdom is a treasure buried in a field, and the man who finds it sells everything he owns to buy the land. The transaction only makes sense if you know what’s in the ground. Not, as Plank puts it, “a begrudging act of surrender, but a joyful act of servitude.”

There’s a second reading of the phrase she likes as much: being found in the field of God’s presence, and staying there. “Giving up everything to remain there.”

Made for One Room

None of these songs arrived as an album. They arrived as chapel services.

SEU Worship is the worship movement at Southeastern University, an Assemblies of God school in Lakeland, Florida, and the group’s records are assembled backward from what already works in the room. Songs get played on campus for months before anyone decides whether they’re worth recording.

“When you hear an album of ours, usually we’ve been playing it all year on our campus,” Plank said. “It’s almost like a yearbook of our year. A snapshot of our year.”

“We play them on campus first to see if they even resonate with our community, or if they even work. And then what’s working in chapel and in our community is usually what makes the records every time.”

It’s a filter that runs in the opposite direction from most of the industry, where a song is written to travel and then handed to a congregation. Plank’s advice to other churches making music is to stop reaching so far.

“It is first and foremost for your community,” she said. “Who did God call you to steward? I can’t steward the nation. I can’t disciple the world.”

Even the writing sessions start there: “What’s the language that our community is missing? What concept do you feel like we’re needing to sing about?”

Rooms That Used to Be Empty

That approach got tested this summer, when SEU Worship — coming off a 10-day outpouring on campus in February that drew national attention — took songs written for one chapel out on its first headlining tour. The group also served as its own setup and teardown crew.

“We set up all the stage design, lighting, all the booths that we had,” Plank said, calling it a boots-on-the-ground experiment and, unexpectedly, a bonding one.

What Shuffit remembers is the singing.

“We were filling a room with young adults and people from all age groups and doing like two hours of worship, only playing our songs,” he said. “Me and Chelsea have both been a part of SEU Worship long enough to know that there were times in the early days where that wasn’t always possible. There wasn’t always a room full of people that could sing our songs.”

“That was a very sobering and humbling realization.”

The song he keeps coming back to isn’t the one Plank almost left off. It’s “Bless the Blood,” written in an unusually small room — just him, Plank and Caylie Bryant.

“We had to fight for it,” he said. Months of it, on and off: leaving it, coming back to it, leaving it, coming back to it. It wasn’t finished until the week of the recording.

“The way that it portrays the sacrifice that Christ made for us, and the power that that has, is some of the most moving lyrical content I’ve ever gotten to be a part of.”

As for the song she tried to leave behind, Plank has noticed where it lands hardest, and it isn’t with students. It’s with the people running things.

“Where I’ve seen it connecting specifically is with other church leaders,” she said. “Because of just remembering the why.”

“It’s just a joy to give up our lives for the Gospel.”

items.title: What Is All This Exorcism Content For?
items.author: Johanna Duncan
items.summary:
Johanna Duncan

Somebody will answer the questions regarding evil when people ask, and better a priest with a stole than an influencer shuffling tarot cards.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Johanna Duncan

I’ll be the first to admit that I’ve truly enjoyed starting my day with breakfast and a long commute to work with Fr. Carlos Martin’s incredible podcast The Exorcist Files playing in the background. If there was an early 2000s movie about my life, the opening scene wouldn’t be a cute hype-up song; viewer discretion would be announced. And when Fr. Martins’s content is not enough, there’s interviews with Fr. Ripperger, there’s Fr. Dan Reehil’s shows Battle Ready and Ask the Exorcist, and so much more. I can attest that the content out there is pretty much endless, and now that it has been so out in the open for a few years, the question arises: What is all this exorcism content for?

Previous generations had the myths and horror movies, we have the exorcists themselves retelling their experiences. There’s nothing new about exorcists and their ministries, but in the last few years, the priests who spend their lives driving out demons went from being the Church’s most guarded (even mysterious) ministers to one of its most bookable guests. We have Fr. Carlos Martins, who built an entire hit podcast around his own case notes, and others followed but mostly as guests in major podcasts. What used to happen behind a rectory door with the blinds drawn is now something many like me have queued up for my morning commute. It is well narrated, dramatized, and downloaded by millions. You get the quality of Hollywood and the education no Sunday school tends to give.

Personally, I grew up exposed to this content from a very young age. My grandfather was a holder (which is a lay person who assists in the deliverance ministry as physical and spiritual support) until his old age didn’t allow him to continue. He always instilled in his children and grandchildren that the worst thing the devil can do is make one believe that neither him nor God are real, and that’s the truly evil thing about him. Everything else, everything we see in movies—the levitations and ugly faces—is just for show. This was the reason he prudently shared some of his experiences, and I perceive that is also the reason exorcists are booking podcasts.

More than any other ministry, becoming a holder is something one gets called to and receives the graces for. In my grandfather’s case, there was no sign-up sheet at his parish. Instead, on a random day, he sat next to a young man in a rectory, and they waited for the priest after Mass. When the priest stepped into the room, the man manifested and launched himself towards the priest, who was caught completely off-guard. In that moment, my grandfather jumped on top of the man and managed to pin him to the ground while the priest got hold of his stole and proceeded to help the inflicted. My grandfather reflected on that moment as his invitation to the ministry, one he hadn’t thought of at all but by mere instinct literally jumped at. After that, the bishop got in contact, and my grandparents joined the ministry. My grandfather was a holder, and my grandmother would pray the Rosary outside.

While my grandfather would never speak on the matter, it was obvious he had a conviction about the importance of being aware of the enemy’s dirty work because people rarely fall into it intentionally; instead, it is mostly driven by naivety, by worshipping things and beings that aren’t God. Some people fall into it (or as the exorcism lingo would say, “open doors”) somewhat unintentionally and sometimes because of our own human brokenness. If we think that our actions don’t have spiritual consequences and engage with things we shouldn’t, we slip into breaking the first commandment: to love God above all things. And by looking around at our world, there’s no doubt that many doors are wide open. That is one of the main reasons for all this exorcism content.

But there is another half of this truth: This is not a topic for everybody. Like every ministry in the Church, this one is a calling, not a curiosity or entertainment alone, and that’s the danger of some of this content. I do think the exorcists are being careful and prudent in how they share the content, but they certainly have no control over what people and the devil himself will do with this information. My grandfather recognized his experiences as a holder were a gift God gave him, and like all gifts from God, he was meant to share it; but slowly, prudently, and considering the state of the person receiving it. And while he shared it with his family, I now recognize that he did not share it equally, since it was not appropriate or necessary for everybody.

Similarly in The Rite, the book by Matt Baglio that later inspired the film, follows the true story of Fr. Gary Thomas, an American priest sent by his bishop to Rome to train in the ministry of exorcism. Before the calling to the priesthood and the ministry of deliverance, Fr. Thomas spent years in his family’s mortuary business, embalming bodies in Los Gatos, California, following his own father into a trade most of us would find unbearable. Looking back, that was not a simple coincidence; it was how God prepared him from childhood for his vocation.

But podcasts are not like that. There’s an overload of information available to unprepared eyes, ears, and, most importantly, hearts.

The Exorcist Files shot to the top of Spotify’s religion and spirituality charts within six days of its January 2023 launch and has stayed high up since. Fr. Chad Ripperger and Fr. Dan Reehil each command online followings in the hundreds of thousands. Exorcism—once the most guarded corner of priestly life—is now something we can not only consume but consume in excess.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Which brings us back to the matter on the table: These are lay people in large numbers learning about something that was never meant to be lay. So what is all this content actually for? I think the honest answer runs in two directions at once, and both are true.

The first direction is a caution, and it’s aimed squarely at whoever is listening. This material is heavy, and it does impact people whether they want it to or not. Fr. Carlos Martins says at the beginning of every episode that discretion is advised, and this is not for everyone. But I am afraid that the disclaimer gets ignored. And when approached with sadistic curiosity and an appetite for shock rather than the desire for understanding, it can genuinely harm you. If suddenly one starts to think that everything is demonic and everything is the devil’s fault, one may slip into unintentionally giving him control of our psyche, our emotions, and eventually, our whole lives. 

There’s also the classic danger that every exorcist is trained to guard against from the first day: untamed curiosity. The fascination with the occult as if it were a spectator sport is one of the more common ways people end up needing an exorcist in the first place. This is largely because we end up amazed by the evil one and his powers, and we lose sight of God’s place. It is important to keep in mind that exorcisms aren’t about the power of demons but about God’s incredible love, mercy, and desire to be close to us. And on our end, we must remember the importance of choosing God freely above all things. So ask yourself before you press play on the next one: Why are you even listening? The exorcists’ work is both possible and successful due to their prudence and restraint, which is what we should maintain as listeners.

The second direction is the reason why the priests keep saying yes to the microphone in the first place. A great many people end up in the devil’s hands not through some dramatic occult ritual but through plain ignorance. Fr. Martins was candid about this when The Exorcist Files launched: A growing share of young adults had drifted from organized religion entirely, and yet a majority of that same age group told pollsters they believed people could become possessed by demons. That gap is exactly where danger awaits: the belief in the demonic with no framework for resisting it, no sacraments, nowhere to turn but Google. Fr. Martins reaches those people—the Catholics and non-Catholics alike. With the practicality of a podcast, he provides the Sunday school education most people never got.

It is also important to keep in mind that the reason we have all this content is not because the exorcists simply woke up on a random day and collectively decided it was time to try the influencer route. Instead, the Church asked them to. Rome is treating this as urgent, and this spring, Pope Leo XIV convened exorcists from around the world for a summit the Church itself framed as a response to a rise in cases driven largely by tarot, witchcraft, and casual occultism going mainstream online. Terms like “manifesting” have become normalized and well marketed into the world of “self-help.” It is presented as innocent, harmless, and even healthy, while it is actually the opposite.

The Vatican has two priorities on the matter at this moment: more priests who are well trained and ready and quality education on the matter so fewer people have to learn the hard way. But there are still many questions about how to best achieve this, and while I think the podcasts are working, they aren’t side-effect-proof, so the tension continues. And while I understand why many don’t want this topic to be mainstream, exorcisms have never actually been absent from popular culture. Therefore, we might as well take the reins and make sure the matter is properly addressed. The fact that a Google search now lands you at The Exorcist Files or an interview with an actual exorcist instead of the trailer of the ’70s film The Exorcist is progress.

William Peter Blatty’s novel-turned-film seared the ministry into the public imagination in 1971 and gave the culture a framework most people still hold: spinning heads, crawling up the walls, a mystery kept firmly in the dark, etc. It has all proven to sell tickets. But it is also entirely wrong about what an exorcism actually is and what it’s for. Measured against that, the current wave of priest-led, theologically careful content isn’t a loss of the Church’s discretion; if anything, I would say it is a recovery. Priests wary of the spotlight agree that silence has a cost of its own because, for better or worse, when the Church goes quiet on this topic, people don’t stop seeking help, they just start seeking it somewhere else. 

That last clause is why the Church has allowed, even encouraged exorcism content. Somebody will answer the questions regarding evil when people ask, and better a priest with a stole than an influencer shuffling tarot cards. While I think it brings an incredible and much needed education to the general public, this is no easy task. I think it is making the work of these exorcists quite difficult. Their schedules are already busy, they are already understaffed, and they must operate at a high level of discipline and humility. 

Fr. Martins has mentioned more than once in his podcast that during an exorcism one should never engage in conversation with a demon, and this same restraint must apply when we talk about them because through conversation we establish relationships. We may even fall into giving them the admiration they seek. Some priests have gotten in trouble for not following this rule, so discussing them in podcasts makes this even more difficult for them.
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

There’s also the fact that the moment the ministry becomes about the man undertaking it rather than the God he’s serving, one is in troubled waters. Undoubtedly, these priests have become celebrities and influencers in their own right, and while (again) this is not a bad thing in itself, it does make their job more difficult. But if difficulty level was the determining factor in what the priests or the Church should do, I don’t think we would have the two-thousand-year-old tradition that we do. Prudence for these priests doesn’t mean silence; it means always staying a servant and steward to the ministry to which God has called them.

The purpose of all this content is to remind us of the first commandment and the dangers of not putting God above all things. Consuming this content should make one want to go to confession and seek the sacraments and closeness to God—not due to fear but out of love and awe for his love and mercy towards us. That is what makes the exorcists’ side-gig as influencers and podcasters worth their precious time. And I do think they are succeeding. I initially discovered The Exorcists Files from a friend who was not attending Mass at the time but had her views and life changed by the podcast and soon after returned to the sacraments. Then I showed the podcast to another friend, and after two years of listening (or shall we say, being catechized), he started going to Mass for the first time in over a decade. The polls claim that Catholicism is on the rise, and I do think all this exorcism content has something to do with it.

My grandfather started sharing his experiences with me at the ripe age of seven when he was also helping prepare me for my First Communion, and like the priests on the podcasts, he did it for the sake of helping me understand the incredible gift of the sacraments.

Whatever you take from these podcasts on your own commute, in your own kitchen, on some ordinary afternoon, instead of pondering whether the devil is real or what his deal is, ponder in gratitude the God who loves us so immensely and is generous in his grace. While we will continue fighting our own battles, he already conquered all evil and won the ultimate war for our sake.

items.title: Saturday, September 5, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus declares that he is Lord of the Sabbath.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
1 Corinthians 4:6b-15

 I have applied all this to Apollos and myself for your benefit, brothers and sisters, so that you may learn through us the meaning of the saying, “Nothing beyond what is written,” so that none of you will be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if it were not a gift?

Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Quite apart from us you have become kings! Indeed, I wish that you had become kings, so that we might be kings with you! For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, as though sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to mortals. We are fools for the sake of Christ, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute. To the present hour we are hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed and beaten and homeless, and we grow weary from the work of our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we speak kindly. We have become like the rubbish of the world, the dregs of all things, to this very day.

I am not writing this to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you might have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers. Indeed, in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.

Psalm
Psalm 145:17-18, 19-20, 21

The Lord is just in all his ways,
    and kind in all his doings.
The Lord is near to all who call on him,
    to all who call on him in truth.
He fulfills the desire of all who fear him;
    he also hears their cry, and saves them.
The Lord watches over all who love him,
    but all the wicked he will destroy.
My mouth will speak the praise of the Lord,
    and all flesh will bless his holy name forever and ever.

Gospel Reading
Luke 6:1-5

One sabbath while Jesus was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked some heads of grain, rubbed them in their hands, and ate them. But some of the Pharisees said, “Why are you doing what is not lawful on the sabbath?” Jesus answered, “Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry? He entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and gave some to his companions?” Then he said to them, “The Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.”

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus declares that he is Lord of the Sabbath.

Again and again, Jesus is portrayed as violating the sacred command to rest on the seventh day. His disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, and many times he cures on the Sabbath, much to the dismay of the protectors of Jewish law.

When challenged, he declares himself Lord of the Sabbath (a breathtaking claim for a Jew to make, since Yahweh alone could be assigned that title) and clarifies that the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath.

In short, he claimed the properly divine prerogative of relativizing the significance of perhaps the defining practice of pious Jews and placing it in subordination to the kingdom of God.
